CMS Medicare Part B Spending by Drug 2024 (data.cms.gov dataset 76a714ad-3a2c-43ac-b76d-9dadf8f7d890, HCPCS J7179, 'Von Willebrand Factor'): $16,183,475.48 over 51 beneficiaries = $317,323.05 per beneficiary, read 2026-11-10. The same disease, which is the comparator rule data/assumptions/jnj_inlexzo.csv sets
column12: no price for VGA039 exists, because it is unapproved. The anchor errs low for a prophylactic: Vonvendi's label covers on-demand bleeding, perioperative management and routine prophylaxis together, so its per-beneficiary spend blends a patient treated around one operation with a patient infused every week of the year, and 51 beneficiaries is thin. The cross-check in the other direction is Hemlibra, the subcutaneous non-factor prophylactic VGA039 most resembles, at $230,046,953 over 438 beneficiaries = $525,221 in the same file (J7170), the figure data/assumptions/rog_hemlibra.csv carries. The true price sits between them and nothing free narrows it

No persistence study for any prophylactic in von Willebrand disease was found

column11: Michael Soucie J, Miller CH, Byams VR, Payne AB, Abe K, Sidonio RF Jr, Kouides PA, 'Occurrence rates of von Willebrand disease among people receiving care in specialized treatment centres in the United States', Haemophilia 2021;27(3):445-453 (doi 10.1111/hae.14263, PMID 33780098, PMC10591267), surveillance on all 24,238 VWD patients who attended a US haemophilia treatment centre over 2012 to 2019: 'Age-adjusted HTC-treated prevalence was 8.6 cases/100,000 (7.2/100,000 for Type 1, 1.2/100,000 for Type 2 and 1.7/million for Type 3)'. Applied to the 340,110,988 US residents of 1 July 2024 (Census), the denominator the book's existing von Willebrand row uses: 0.000086 x 340,110,988 = 29,250. This is the same paper the book already cites for 'von Willebrand Disease, Type 3' on Hemlibra, read one line up for all types, so the two rows rest on one measurement
column12: a lower bound, and the paper says why: it counts only people receiving care at a haemophilia treatment centre, and its own conclusion is that the rates 'are likely strongly influenced by differences in rates of diagnosis'. The CDC Community Counts HTC Population Profile is the same population counted differently, 33,456 people over 1/1/2012 to 9/29/2023, which is a period count rather than an age-adjusted rate and is not carried here. The 1% of the population sometimes quoted for VWD is a laboratory phenotype, not a prescribable pool, and is not used

column11: stated at nil, the convention the book already uses on 38 rows where a prevalent pool has no usable US inflow. Soucie 2021 reports HTC-treated incidence per 100,000 live births by sex and type (type 1 26.2 for women against 9.9 for men, type 2 2.2 against 1.4, type 3 'slight' difference) and no combined all-type rate, so a single incidence cannot be formed from it without assuming a sex split of births. forecast.pool_rule reads a nil inflow as a closed pool
column12: nil is a modelling statement, not a claim that nobody is born with the disease. The book's type 3 row does carry an inflow, 9 a year, built from the same paper's 'overall HTC-treated incidence of 2.4 per million live births' for type 3 alone; that figure does not scale to all types

column11: the types 2 and 3 share of the same Soucie 2021 age-adjusted rates: (1.2 per 100,000 for type 2 plus 1.7 per million, which is 0.17 per 100,000, for type 3) over 8.6 per 100,000 for all VWD = 1.37 / 8.6 = 0.159302, about 4,660 patients. Types 2 and 3 are the qualitative and the severe quantitative forms, which is where a bleeding phenotype heavy enough for routine prophylaxis sits. VIVID-6 (NCT07115004) admits 'VWD of any type' but requires a 'historical annualized bleeding rate (ABR; excluding menstrual bleeds and bleeds under the skin) of both untreated and treated bleeds >= 12 per year'
column12: the weakest row in this file and the one to argue with. It is a cut by VWD type, not by the trial's bleeding rate, because no published US share of VWD patients with an ABR of 12 or more was found in this session. It reads high: a bleed a month is well above what a typical type 2 patient records, and the trial also excludes anyone already on weekly VWF concentrate prophylaxis, a cut not taken here. It reads low on one axis only, in that severe type 1 patients can meet the bleeding criterion and are not counted. Replace it with a published ABR distribution if one appears

column11: copied from the judgement the book already holds for the closest claim it contains, Hemlibra's 'von Willebrand Disease, Type 3' layer: a subcutaneous non-factor prophylactic displacing intravenous von Willebrand factor concentrate infused one to three times a week. The case for a high share is the same convenience argument that took emicizumab to the majority of US haemophilia A prophylaxis. The case for a low one is also the same and is why the number is not higher: VGA039 is an anti-protein S antibody that raises thrombin generation, so like emicizumab it restores coagulation without replacing von Willebrand factor, and it cannot correct the platelet adhesion defect that drives the mucocutaneous, gastrointestinal and menstrual bleeding these patients suffer. Those bleeds would still need concentrate, which is a reason to prescribe alongside rather than instead
column12: the direction it errs in: high, and it is not anchored on a measured reach because the book holds none for any prophylactic in von Willebrand disease. The nearest measurement is Hemlibra's own, 438 Medicare Part B beneficiaries in 2024 against a US haemophilia A pool of 20,129 (CMS Part B spending by drug and data/epidemiology.csv), 2.2%, but Medicare covers a small and old slice of a congenital bleeding disorder population so that is a floor on the channel rather than a share of the disease. A peak share is settled by years of sales
